clue.text: Defender was hard, leading to repercussion

parts.note: a back is a defending player in football or rugby
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A footballer's tough defending had consequences later in the match.
explanation.definitionFit: Backwash is the unwelcome aftermath of an event, a synonym for its repercussion.

clue.text: Equip expert to limit error in court

indicators.note: to limit something is to bound it, so the expert's letters enclose the rest

parts.note: an ace is an expert

indicators.note: an error in the word court means its letters are wrongly arranged

explanation.surface: A legal expert is told to keep mistakes in the courtroom to a minimum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'error in' is the anagram signal, and 'to limit' has the expert's letters split around the result.
explanation.definitionFit: To accoutre someone is to outfit them with gear, a formal synonym for equipping.

clue.text: Tense exploit held up by Austrian artist

indicators.note: in a down clue, held up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
to milk something is to exploit it

explanation.surface: A painter from Vienna, nervous and taken advantage of, is delayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held up' reverses TMILK, giving the painter Gustav Klimt.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Klimt was the Viennese Secession painter of The Kiss, an example of an Austrian artist.

clue.text: Fruitful aspects of flight, some say

definitions.text: Fruitful aspects of flight, some say

parts.words: Fruitful aspects of flight, some say
parts.note: Cockney rhyming slang for stairs, the parts of a flight, uses two fruits; 'some say' points to the Cockney speakers

explanation.surface: The fruit-bearing parts of an aeroplane journey, as some people put it.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang, a London dialect, a phrase stands for the word it rhymes with: here two fruits rhyme with stairs, and a flight is a set of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the rhyming-slang term for stairs, which make up a flight, and it names two fruits.

clue.text: Dispersed the endless pain around and about the liver

indicators.note: letters dispersed are scattered and regathered in a new order
endless means the final letter of pain is cut off

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for around

explanation.surface: Something scattered the never-ending ache in and around a patient's liver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims the pain before 'Dispersed' mixes it with 'the'. 'around' is not a container signal here but circa's abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Hepatic is the medical adjective for anything relating to the liver, so it means concerning that organ.

clue.text: Method to limit volume of the sea, perhaps

indicators.note: to limit is to enclose within bounds, so the method's letters go around the volume

parts.note: a way is a method

explanation.surface: A technique for controlling how loud the ocean is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks the sea as just one example of something that can be wavy.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea's surface is typically rippled with waves, an example of something described as wavy.

clue.text: Piece dedicated to Council of Europe and staff

parts.note: a work is a piece of art or music
something dedicated to a person is for them
CE is the abbreviation for the Council of Europe

explanation.surface: A composition dedicated to a European body and its employees.
explanation.definitionFit: A workforce is the body of people employed somewhere, a synonym for its staff.

clue.text: Subordinate against attack I abandoned

parts.note: V, short for versus, means against

indicators.note: abandoned means the letter I is left out of the attack word

parts.note: to assail is to attack

explanation.surface: A junior officer, opposed to the assault, says he gave it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I abandoned' tells you the letter I leaves the attack word.
explanation.definitionFit: A vassal held land under a feudal lord, so he was that lord's underling.

clue.text: Second busy time with Queen repeatedly receiving disdain where pundits opine

indicators.note: receiving means the Queens hold the disdain, so it sits between the two copies

parts.note: peak time is the busiest period
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen
scorn is disdain
repeatedly means the Queen's ER is given a second time

explanation.surface: A rush hour moment, the monarch twice getting contempt, in a place where commentators hold forth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repeatedly' gives the Queen twice and 'receiving' sets the disdain between the two copies. Speakers' Corner is the spot in London's Hyde Park where anyone may stand and make public speeches.
explanation.definitionFit: Speakers' Corner is a famous open-air spot for public speaking, so it is a place for airing opinions.

clue.text: Small crease? Don't be too expansive

parts.note: a crimp is a small fold or crease

explanation.surface: A little wrinkle, with advice not to make it too big.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expansive' here means generous with money, not physically large.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrimp is to economise and avoid being lavish, so the command urges not spending freely.

clue.text: Old paper: Wage demand cut after intervention by Prince

indicators.note: intervention by the Prince means he steps in among the wage's letters

parts.note: pay is a wage

indicators.note: cut means the demand word loses its final letter

parts.note: a rush is a sudden demand for goods

explanation.surface: An old newspaper reports a pay claim was trimmed after a royal stepped in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intervention by' places the prince inside the wage, and 'cut' docks the demand's last letter. 'after' is only a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Papyrus was the reed-based writing material of ancient Egypt, the ancestor of modern paper.

clue.text: Measure of intelligence, say, not quite sorted out

indicators.note: sorted out means the letters of the preceding words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: An IQ test score, claimed to be not entirely put in order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorted out' rearranges NOT QUITE. 'say' signals that the IQ is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Q in IQ stands for quotient, a ratio of mental age to real age; IQ is an example of one.

clue.text: Some light obtained after a very loud brawl

indicators.note: after means the light comes behind the earlier pieces in the answer

parts.note: FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A beam of light was produced following a noisy fight.
explanation.definitionFit: An affray is a fight in a public place, a legal term for a brawl.

clue.text: Obvious uproar at callers being abused

parts.note: a cry is an outcry or uproar

indicators.note: being abused means the letters are mistreated and thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: It's plain there was an outcry when phone callers got insulted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being abused' is the anagram signal working on 'at callers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something crystal-clear is completely plain and easy to understand, a synonym for obvious.

clue.text: Chest covering for a chest, possibly (male not female)

indicators.note: possibly means the letters could be arranged in another way
male not female says one letter for male takes the place of the letter for female

explanation.surface: A garment for the chest, the bracket noting it is men's wear, not women's.
explanation.walkthrough: '(male not female)' swaps the F of FOR A CHEST for M, giving MORACHEST; 'possibly' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stomacher was an ornamental panel worn over the chest and stomach, chiefly in Tudor dress.

clue.text: Pain after one European abandons environmentally-sound grape variety

indicators.note: after means the pain comes behind the shortened green word
abandons means one E leaves the green word

parts.note: green means environmentally sound
E is the abbreviation for European
an ache is a pain

explanation.surface: Discomfort follows when a European gives up an eco-friendly grape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandons' drops just one of the two Es, and 'after' puts the pain at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenache is a red wine grape grown widely in Spain and southern France, an example of a variety.

clue.text: Traveller's joy: bar, and models cavorting

indicators.note: cavorting means jumping about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A happy travelling salesman's pleasure: a pub and dancing fashion models.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traveller's joy' looks like a pleasure on a journey, but it is the name of a wild clematis. 'cavorting' rearranges BAR AND MODELS.
explanation.definitionFit: Old man's beard is another common name for wild clematis, so named for its fluffy seed heads.

clue.text: Partner mostly upset about wife in European city

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the wife
upset means the letters are knocked over into a new order
mostly means the last letter of partner is dropped

explanation.surface: A spouse, quite unsettled about his wife, in a city on the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims PARTNER to PARTNE, 'upset' rearranges it, and 'about' wraps it round W.
explanation.definitionFit: Antwerp is a major port city in Belgium, an example of a city in Europe.

clue.text: Spook seen around your university is rather sweet

indicators.note: seen around means the spy's letters are placed on both sides of the rest

parts.note: a spook is slang for a spy

explanation.surface: A secret agent spotted near your campus is a bit cloying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen around' has the spook enclose the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Syrupy describes something thick with sugar, so it means quite sugary or cloying.

clue.text: Fellow returned, concealed by extra sobriquet

indicators.note: concealed by means the reversed fellow sits inside the extra

parts.note: a bye is an extra in cricket, a run not scored off the bat

indicators.note: returned means the fellow's letters are sent back the other way

parts.note: a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A man came back, hidden behind an additional nickname.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reverses the fellow and 'concealed by' hides him in the extra, a cricket term for a run not scored off the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: A byname is a secondary name or nickname, a synonym for a sobriquet.

clue.text: Instrumentalist's time in Paris good, moving into another city

indicators.note: moving into means the French word goes inside the city

parts.note: Rome is a city other than Paris
bon is French for good

explanation.surface: A musician has a good time in Paris before relocating to a different city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving into' puts the French word inside the other city. The definition is possessive: the trombone is the instrumentalist's instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A trombone belongs to the player of it, so the brass instrument can stand for what is that musician's.

clue.text: British eggs seeing upturn? Excellent!

indicators.note: in a down clue, seeing upturn means the eggs are read from the bottom up

parts.note: ova are eggs

explanation.surface: Egg production in Britain is rising: great news!
explanation.walkthrough: 'seeing upturn' reverses the eggs, upwards in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravo is an exclamation of applause, an interjection of approval like 'Well done!'.

clue.text: Bring down our hens for treatment

indicators.note: for treatment means the letters are worked over and rearranged

explanation.surface: Kill off our sick chickens to treat them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for treatment' rearranges OUR HENS.
explanation.definitionFit: To unhorse a rider is to throw them from the saddle, literally to topple them to the ground.

clue.text: Subtlety in article penned by religious figure going to church

indicators.note: penned by means the article is enclosed by the nun

parts.note: a nun is a religious woman
a is the indefinite article
CE is the abbreviation for the Church of England

explanation.surface: A nun on her way to church writes a fine-shaded piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penned by' has the religious figure enclose the article.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuance is a fine shade of meaning or difference, a synonym for a subtlety.

clue.text: Colour specialist: ultimately every colour of the rainbow is seen round about

indicators.note: is seen round means the reversed colour goes around the final letter
about means the rainbow colour is turned back to front

parts.note: red is one of the seven colours of the rainbow

indicators.note: ultimately means the final letter of every is taken

explanation.surface: A colour expert notes every hue of the rainbow eventually appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses RED to DER, and 'is seen round' puts Y, the last of 'every', inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A dyer colours fabric for a living, so is a craftsman expert in colouring.

clue.text: Chaucerian pilgrim finished interrupting Father and Bishop

parts.note: pa is a familiar name for father

indicators.note: interrupting means the finished word breaks into the father-and-bishop pair

parts.note: RR, Right Reverend, is the title of a bishop
done means finished

explanation.surface: A medieval pilgrim stopped talking, cutting in on a priest and a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interrupting' puts the finished word between Father and Bishop; RR, Right Reverend, is a bishop's style.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pardoner, a seller of indulgences, tells one of the stories in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.
